name: Lotus Sutra
info: The Lotus Sūtra is a Mahāyāna Buddhist scripture by unknown Indian authors, composed in phases from about the 1st century CE, and the main text of the Tiantai, Tendai and Nichiren schools of East Asia.

facts.made: Unknown authors, likely highly educated Buddhist monks of India (Lopez); Mahāyāna Buddhists hold that it records the teaching of Shakyamuni Buddha at Vulture Peak; possibly of the Mahāsāṃghika school (Roberts)
facts.form: A Mahāyāna sūtra in prose and verse, 28 chapters in Kumārajīva's Chinese version; first written probably in a Prakrit later Sanskritised; Chinese translations of 286, 406 and 601 CE
facts.where: Sanskrit manuscripts survive, including Nepalese copies; the Chinese, Tibetan and other translations are read in East Asian temples and homes; Dunhuang held a thousand copies sealed in the 11th century
facts.known: The One Vehicle; skilful means; the parable of the burning house; the immeasurable lifespan of the Buddha; the jewelled stupa; the Dragon King's daughter; the chapter on Avalokiteśvara; the chanted title Namu Myōhō Renge Kyō

t: The sūtra teaches that the many Buddhist paths are skilful means within a single One Vehicle that leads all beings to Buddhahood.
It presents the Buddha's lifespan as immeasurable: his death is described as a teaching device, and he is said to remain active in the world.
Little known in India, it became the main scripture of the Tiantai, Tendai and Nichiren schools and shaped the art, poetry and devotion of East Asia.
dyk: In the Japanese poetry compendium Kanwa taisho myoho renge-kyo, drawn from more than 120 collections of the Heian period, over 1360 poems refer to the Lotus Sūtra in their titles alone.
ev: Yoisho Tamura dates the first stage of composition, chapters 2 to 9, to about this time
Dharmarakṣa's team completes the first Chinese translation at Chang'an
Kumārajīva's team completes the translation that becomes the standard one in East Asian Buddhism
Jñānagupta and Dharmagupta translate the Supplemented Lotus Sūtra, a revision of Kumārajīva's text
The Japanese emperor founds a network of provincial nunneries, the Temples for the Eradication of Sins through the Lotus
Matteo Ricci mentions the sūtra and denounces its teaching, one of the first mentions by a westerner
Hendrik Kern publishes his English translation from Nepalese Sanskrit manuscripts in the Sacred Books of the East

sections.origins:
The Lotus Sūtra (Sanskrit Saddharma Puṇḍarīka Sūtra, "Sūtra on the White Lotus of the True Dharma") is a Mahāyāna Buddhist sūtra, a discourse attributed to the Buddha. Mahāyāna Buddhists receive it as the teaching of Shakyamuni Buddha, given at a gathering on Vulture Peak. Scholars study it as a text of unknown authorship. According to Donald S. Lopez Jr., it is clearly a work of high literary quality, and its authors were likely highly educated Buddhist monks, fully at ease among the doctrines and tropes of Buddhism as it existed in India at the time.

According to Peter Alan Roberts, the sūtra may have had its origin among the Mahāsāṃghika school and may have been written in a middle Indic language, a prakrit, that was later Sanskritised. That the original was in prakrit remains a contested claim among both secular and religious historians. For the first Chinese translation, it was at first held that the source was in Sanskrit, but the view that it was a Prakrit text has gained widespread acceptance.

The sūtra was often cited in Indian scholarly treatises and compendiums, and the number of surviving manuscripts and fragments suggests it was copied often. Jonathan Silk judges that its influence in India may have been limited, though it is a prominent scripture in East Asian Buddhism.
sections.content:
The sūtra is presented as a drama in several mythological scenes. Sangharakshita observes that it uses the whole cosmos for its stage, employs many mythological beings as actors and speaks almost exclusively in the language of images. Gene Reeves describes three parts: the One Vehicle of the Wonderful Dharma, the everlasting life of the Buddha, and the activities of human beings, the bodhisattva way. Kumārajīva's Chinese version has 28 chapters.

Two teachings have been especially influential. The first is the One Vehicle (ekayāna): the three vehicles to awakening are skilful means (upāya), the many ways Buddhas adapt their teaching to their hearers, and all lead to Buddhahood. The Buddha explains this through parables, among them the burning house, in which a father coaxes his children out with the promise of toy carts and gives them one large cart instead. The second is that the Buddha's lifespan is immeasurable. In chapter 16 he says he attained Buddhahood countless aeons ago and only appears to pass into final nirvāṇa, as the doctor in a parable feigns death to bring his sons to take medicine.

The text also says that all beings can become Buddhas. Chapter 11 shows a jewelled stupa rising from the earth with the Buddha Prabhūtaratna inside, and in chapter 12 the Dragon King's daughter becomes a Buddha. Chapter 25 praises Avalokiteśvara, who hears the cries of the world.
sections.making:
According to Lopez, the general scholarly consensus is that the sūtra took shape in four phases. The first layer is chapters 2 to 9, which Seishi Karashima thinks began as verses transmitted orally in a Prakrit dialect; he assigns the prose of the same chapters to a second phase. In Lopez's account the third phase added chapter 1 and chapters 10 to 22, except chapter 12, and the fourth added chapters 23 to 27 and the Devadatta chapter, with chapter 28 later still. Karashima divides the later layers differently.

Stephen F. Teiser and Jacqueline Stone note a consensus about the stages but not about their dates. Yoisho Tamura argues that chapters 2 to 9 were completed around 50 CE, chapters 10 to 21 added around 100 CE, and a third stage placed around 150 CE. In the Sanskrit versions and the alternative Chinese translation chapter 22 is the last; Shioiri suggests that an earlier version ended there and that chapters 23 to 28 were inserted later.

Different versions divide the text differently, and the chapter summary used by scholars follows Kumārajīva's expanded Chinese version, the most widely translated.
sections.reception:
In India the One Vehicle was received unevenly. The Madhyamaka school embraced it, while Yogācāra thinkers read the sūtra as provisional, holding that when the Buddha called the Buddha vehicle the one vehicle he meant that it was the supreme vehicle. According to Paramārtha (499 to 569 CE) there were over fifty Indian commentaries; only one survives, in Chinese, and it is attributed to Vasubandhu, though scholars question this.

In China, Daosheng (355 to 434) wrote the oldest surviving commentary, and Daoxuan (596 to 667) called it the most important sūtra in China. Zhiyi (538 to 597), a patriarch of the Tiantai school, divided it into a trace teaching and a fundamental teaching, and wrote the Profound Meaning of the Lotus Sūtra and the Words and Phrases of the Lotus Sūtra. In Japan, Saichō (767 to 822) brought Tiantai as the Tendai school. Nichiren (1222 to 1282) held that the title is the essence of the sūtra and taught the chanting of the daimoku, Namu Myōhō Renge Kyō. He judged other schools mistaken, and his debates led to persecution. Dōgen (1200 to 1253) wrote that all other sūtras are its servants.

Jacqueline Stone and Stephen Teiser write that it is perhaps no exaggeration to say it has been the most influential Buddhist scripture in East Asia.
sections.survival:
Three Chinese translations survive. Dharmarakṣa's team translated it at Chang'an in 286 CE, during the Western Jin. Kumārajīva's team produced a version in seven fascicles in 406 CE, which superseded it and became the standard translation in East Asian Buddhism; according to Jean-Noël Robert he relied heavily on the earlier one. His version lacked the Devadatta chapter, which Dharmarakṣa's had. The third, the Supplemented Lotus Sūtra of the Wonderful Dharma (601 CE), by Jñānagupta and Dharmagupta, is a revision of Kumārajīva's text that restored the Devadatta chapter, various verses and the end of chapter 25. Those elements were later added back to Kumārajīva's text.

In China the core sūtra was traditionally compiled with two others, the Innumerable Meanings Sūtra and the Samantabhadra Meditation Sūtra, as the Threefold Lotus Sūtra. An Indian version was translated into Tibetan in the reign of King Ralpachen (r. 815 to 838), and it most closely matches the Chinese version of Jñānagupta and Dharmagupta and the Nepalese Sanskrit version. A thousand copies of the text were sealed in the Dunhuang caves in the 11th century. The Chinese text has also been translated into Uighur, Tangut and, more recently, colloquial Chinese, Japanese, Vietnamese and Korean.
sections.legacy:
Practice centred on the sūtra itself: receiving, reading, reciting, copying, explaining and honouring it. Memorising it became a requirement for monastic ordination at various points in Chinese history, and Huixiang's Accounts of the Propagation of the Lotus Sūtra, from about the 7th century, belongs to a popular genre of miracle stories. In the 8th century the Japanese emperor established a network of provincial nunneries, the Temples for the Eradication of Sins through the Lotus, to protect the royal family and the state. Chapter 25 fed devotion to Guanyin, while the self-immolation of Bodhisattva Medicine King in chapter 23 inspired a controversial tradition of burning parts of the body.

The scene of Shakyamuni and Prabhūtaratna seated together became, in the fifth century, arguably the most popular theme of Chinese Buddhist art, and the sūtra figures in The Tale of Genji and The Dream of the Red Chamber. The Japanese writer Kenji Miyazawa devoted himself to it. In the West, Eugene Burnouf completed a French translation in 1839, published in 1852; an English version of one chapter appeared in 1844, and Hendrik Kern's full translation in 1884. Modern groups such as Soka Gakkai, which takes an exclusivist approach, and Risshō Kōsei Kai, which is inclusive and ecumenical, carry it worldwide.

summary: The Lotus Sūtra is a Mahāyāna scripture of unknown Indian authorship, composed in phases from about the 1st century CE. It teaches one path to Buddhahood and a Buddha of immeasurable life, and became the main text of the Tiantai, Tendai and Nichiren schools.

notes: Article's start date: only Tamura's c. 50 CE for chapters 2-9 is given; scholars disagree on dating of the strata, so start 50 with circa true.

The article gives Tamura's third stage as chapters 22-27 around 150 CE, which does not match his earlier 'expanded by chapters 10-21 around 100 CE' and Lopez's fourth phase; I gave Tamura's dates as the article states them.
Article says Devadatta chapter is chapter 12 in Kumarajiva's numbering but 'chapter 11' in Karashima's Sanskrit layer note; left the Karashima detail out.

The article says Kumarajiva's version is missing the Devadatta chapter yet gives 28 chapters including chapter 12 Devadatta; the article's chapter overview follows the 'expanded' version. I said 28 chapters for the expanded version only.
Dogen's death year (1253) is given only through his dates 1200-1253; 'final days' event is dated 1253 by that.
Article has 'Tathagatha' and 'Hinayana Nirvana' wording; left out the latter.

Left out: chapter 12's transformation of the Dragon King's daughter into a male bodhisattva, and the 'king of all sutras' simile, as they invite comparative ranking or contested gender readings; the article's claim that the sutra declares rejecters will be reborn in hell was also left out.
The article's 'perhaps the most influential' claims (Stone and Teiser) are attributed and kept to one sentence.
References left empty for the editor.
